questions.q: Why does Mara compare the raw account lists instead of just comparing the two counts, 14 and 19?
options: Because the counts alone cannot distinguish a clean superset from a partial overlap with different accounts on each side -- each scenario has a different root cause
Because counts are always unreliable in Python
Because Howard Okonjo requires account-level detail in every report
Because the audit report doesn't include a total count
questions.explain: A count of 14 versus 19 is consistent with several very different underlying situations -- only comparing the actual accounts, not the totals, tells you which one you're actually in.

questions.q: What three groupings does Mara's set comparison produce?
options: High risk, medium risk, low risk
Accounts in both lists, accounts only in the audit's list, and accounts only in the automation's list
Azure accounts, AWS accounts, and shared accounts
Admin accounts, read-only accounts, and disabled accounts
questions.explain: The reconciliation is a standard set comparison: intersection (in both), and each side's unique difference (only in audit, only in automation).

questions.q: What does the comparison actually find?
options: All 14 audit accounts are also in the automation's list; zero accounts are only in the audit's list; 5 accounts are only in the automation's list
The two lists share only 9 accounts in common
3 accounts are only in the audit's list and 8 are only in the automation's list
The lists have no accounts in common at all
questions.explain: The automation's 19-account list fully contains the audit's 14, plus 5 additional accounts the audit's method never saw -- a clean superset, not a conflicting result.

questions.q: What does "the automation's result is a strict superset of the audit's" rule out?
options: That either tool made a data error or that the two methods are looking at two different, inconsistent populations of accounts
That the OT/SCADA segment exists at all
That Mara's automation uses Python
That Howard Okonjo needs to be briefed
questions.explain: Because every audit account also appears in the automation's list, the discrepancy can't be a miscount or mismatched scope on either side -- it's consistent and structural, which points toward a methodology explanation rather than an error.

questions.q: After this lesson's comparison, what specific open question remains going into Lesson 14?
options: Whether the audit's count of 14 was even correct
Who are the 5 accounts only in the automation's list, and how did each of them get standing admin access to the OT/SCADA segment outside either group
Whether the zero-trust segmentation pilot has failed
Whether Howard Okonjo approved the audit's scope
questions.explain: The set comparison turns a vague discrepancy into a precise, answerable question -- identifying and tracing the origin of exactly 5 named accounts -- which Lesson 14 investigates directly.
